legal.name: Home-based private school (file a Private School Affidavit)
legal.description: The parent establishes a private school in the home and files the annual Private School Affidavit (PSA, also called the R-4) with the California Department of Education. Children enrolled in a full-time private day school are exempt from public school compulsory attendance under Ed Code 48222. CDE lists the home-based private school as one of the ways to educate a child at home. Filing is a registration, not a license or approval: CDE does not verify the information or evaluate curriculum.
requirements: File the Private School Affidavit online with CDE every school year (statutory filing period October 1-15; CDE's online system is open roughly August 1 through June 30 so new and mid-year schools can file when they start). If you file early in August/September you do not need to file again in October.
Offer instruction in English in the several branches of study required to be taught in the public schools (Ed Code 48222; see Ed Code 51210 and 51220 for grades 1-6 and 7-12 areas of study).
Instruction must be by persons capable of teaching (Ed Code 48222); no teaching credential is required for the parent.
Keep an attendance register that clearly indicates every absence of a half day or more (Ed Code 48222).
Keep current and available at the school: the courses of study offered, and the names and addresses of faculty with a record of each one's educational qualifications (Ed Code 33190).
Students must be ages 6-18 within compulsory education range; the school selects and provides all curricular and instructional materials (CDE).
Criminal record summary requirement of Ed Code 44237 does not apply to a parent working exclusively with his or her own children.
pros: Maximum freedom over curriculum, schedule, worldview (including religious materials) and teaching methods.
No reporting to the school district and no state testing or Physical Fitness Test requirement.
Immunization requirements of H&S Code 120335 do not apply to pupils in a home-based private school.
Parent issues own transcripts, diploma and (as principal) can generally issue work permits to students other than their own children (CDE work permit FAQ).
cons: No public funding; family pays all curriculum, classes and testing costs.
Parent carries full record-keeping and high school transcript/diploma responsibility; some colleges, employers and the military scrutinize home-issued diplomas more closely.
Not eligible for public-school-only programs (e.g., California State Parks Free Fourth Grade Pass, CCAP dual enrollment partnerships, state testing).
Filing information (school name, address of record) is submitted under penalty of perjury and schools with six or more students appear in public CDE data.
legal.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 (affidavit and records), 48222 (private full-time day school exemption), 44237 (criminal record summary, parent exemption), H&S Code 120335(f) (immunization exemption)

legal.name: Private School Satellite Program (PSP)
legal.description: The family enrolls the child in an existing private school that operates an independent study / home-study program. The PSP (not the family) files the Private School Affidavit and is legally the child's school; the parent teaches at home under the PSP's policies. CDE describes this option as enrolling 'through an existing private school that offers online learning or independent study options.' PSPs range from record-keeping-only services to full-service programs with classes, counseling, transcripts and accreditation.
requirements: Enroll with a PSP that has filed a current Private School Affidavit with CDE (verify the PSP appears in the CDE private school data or ask for a copy of its filing).
Complete the PSP's enrollment forms, statement of intent, and records release/transfer request.
Submit whatever attendance, course lists, grades or work logs the PSP requires so it can maintain the Ed Code 33190 / 48222 records.
Pay any enrollment or service fees set by the PSP (fees vary widely; some are low-cost).
pros: PSP files the PSA and maintains official cumulative records, so family paperwork is lighter.
Transcripts and diplomas are issued by an established private school; some PSPs are accredited (e.g., WASC) which can help with college admissions.
Same curriculum freedom as a home-based private school, including religious materials.
Often provides community: field trips, classes, graduation ceremonies, counselor support.
cons: Costs money (tuition/fees) and no public funds for curriculum.
Must follow the PSP's own rules (reporting deadlines, required subjects, statement of faith for some).
Quality and accreditation vary; families must vet the PSP themselves.
Not eligible for public-school-only programs.
legal.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 and 48222 (the PSP is the private school that files and keeps records)

legal.name: Public charter school independent study (homeschool charter)
legal.description: The child enrolls in a nonclassroom-based public charter school and completes coursework at home under independent study, supervised by a credentialed teacher of record (often called an Educational Specialist or Supervising Teacher). The student is a public school student. Many homeschool charters provide per-student 'instructional funds' that the school spends (through approved vendors) on curriculum, classes and materials for the family.
requirements: Enroll in a charter school authorized to offer nonclassroom-based independent study (Ed Code 47600 et seq.; independent study under Ed Code 51745-51749.6 and 47612.5).

Sign a written independent study master agreement before instruction begins (Ed Code 51747) covering objectives, methods, assignment frequency, evaluation, duration, and the right to return to classroom instruction.

Meet regularly with the credentialed supervising teacher; provide work samples/learning records each learning period so the school can document attendance through student work product (Ed Code 51747, 5 CCR 11700 et seq.).
Participate in required state testing (CAASPP/ELPAC as applicable) and the Physical Fitness Test in tested grades (Ed Code 60640, 60800).
Use only secular, standards-aligned materials when purchased with public funds; charter schools must be nonsectarian (Ed Code 47605).
Charter cannot give the family funds or any other thing of value directly for independent study (Ed Code 51747.3); purchases are made by the school.
pros: Public funding: no tuition, and many charters provide instructional funds for curriculum, enrichment classes, lessons and supplies.
Credentialed teacher support, special education services and IEPs, counseling, and an accredited public school transcript/diploma (A-G courses at many).
Students are public school students and qualify for public-school programs (e.g., California State Parks Free Fourth Grade Pass, CCAP dual enrollment partnerships).
Immunization requirements do not apply to independent study pupils who receive no classroom-based instruction (H&S 120335(f)).
cons: Must follow state standards, testing, and the charter's reporting/work-sample requirements; less autonomy.
Public funds cannot buy religious curriculum (constitutional challenge Woolard v. Thurmond was pending at the U.S. Supreme Court on cert in late 2026).
Funding amounts, vendor lists and policies differ by charter and can change with state budget or charter renewal.
Families receiving public funds are ineligible for some private homeschool grants (e.g., HSLDA Curriculum Grant).
legal.legal_basis: Ed Code 47600 et seq. (Charter Schools Act), 47612.5, 47634.2 (nonclassroom-based funding determinations), 51745-51749.6 (independent study), 51747.3; 5 CCR 11700-11704

legal.name: Private tutor holding a valid California teaching credential
legal.description: A child may be exempted from public school attendance if instructed by a private tutor (which can be the parent) who holds a valid California teaching credential for the grade level taught. No affidavit filing is required for this option when the Ed Code 48224 conditions are met.
requirements: Tutor holds a valid California state credential for the grade level taught (Ed Code 48224).
Instruction in the several branches of study required in public schools, in English.
At least 3 hours a day for 175 days each calendar year, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. (Ed Code 48224).
Keep attendance records; keep a copy of the credential on file.
pros: No Private School Affidavit filing required.
Full curriculum freedom; useful for credentialed-teacher parents.
Simple legal footing that is well established in statute.
cons: Requires a current California teaching credential appropriate to each child's grade level (most parents do not hold one).
Statutory minimum hours/days and the 8 a.m.-4 p.m. window are less flexible.
Hiring an outside credentialed tutor full-time is expensive.
No public funding; tutor is not a school so diplomas/transcripts need separate planning.

legal.name: Public school district independent study
legal.description: The child stays enrolled in the local school district (or county office of education) and completes work at home through the district's independent study program, under a credentialed supervising teacher. Since 2021-22, every school district and county office of education must offer independent study (with limited exceptions). Short-term and long-term independent study are available; the district provides curriculum.
requirements: Enroll in (or remain in) the district and request placement in its independent study program.
Sign a written independent study agreement before instruction begins (Ed Code 51747), including the student's right to return to in-person instruction.
Complete assignments and submit work product; participate in required synchronous instruction / live interaction as set out in Ed Code 51747 (requirements vary by grade span).
Participate in state testing (CAASPP, ELPAC, Physical Fitness Test in tested grades).
Use district-provided or district-approved curriculum.
pros: Free; curriculum, textbooks and often devices provided.
Stays in the public system: district diploma, IEP/504 services, access to some campus activities and programs.
Easy to return to the classroom; good for short-term or transitional homeschooling.
Eligible for public-school-only programs and CCAP dual enrollment partnerships.
cons: Least curriculum freedom; must follow district materials, pacing and standards.
Regular teacher check-ins, live instruction and testing requirements.
Program quality and flexibility vary greatly by district.
Usually no discretionary 'instructional funds' like those offered by many homeschool charters.
legal.legal_basis: Ed Code 51745-51749.6 (independent study, as amended by AB 130 (2021) and later budget trailer bills); 5 CCR 11700 et seq.

paperwork.name: Private School Affidavit (PSA / R-4)
paperwork.deadline: Statutory filing period October 1-15 each year; CDE online system opens about August 1 and stays open through June 30, so a school starting mid-year files when it begins. Filing in August/September counts; no second October filing needed.
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190; Ed Code 48222
paperwork.description: Online registration filed under penalty of perjury with the California Department of Education listing the school name/address, directors/officers, enrollment by grade and other required information. Filing is not a license or approval. Print/save the confirmation and keep a copy (CDE recommends retaining a copy). Schools opened in July must wait until the August filing period opens.

paperwork.name: Copy of filed Private School Affidavit / confirmation
paperwork.legal_basis: CDE PSA FAQ recommendation; Ed Code 48222 (district may verify affidavit before accepting the exemption)
paperwork.description: Keep a printed or PDF copy of every year's affidavit. It is your proof of the compulsory attendance exemption if a district, truancy officer, or another school asks, and helps later with transcripts and records requests.

paperwork.name: Attendance register
paperwork.frequency: daily, kept for each school year
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 48222
paperwork.description: A register of pupil attendance that clearly indicates every absence of a half day or more. A simple calendar or spreadsheet per student is sufficient. California sets no minimum number of days for private schools, but many families track 175-180 days.

paperwork.name: Attendance records (PSP)
paperwork.frequency: per PSP schedule (often monthly, per semester or annually)
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 48222 (the PSP, as the private school, must keep the register)
paperwork.description: PSP families record attendance at home and turn it in to the PSP, which keeps the official register. Keep your own copy.

paperwork.name: Attendance record (credentialed tutor)
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 48224
paperwork.description: Document that instruction met the statutory minimum of at least 3 hours a day for 175 days each calendar year, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m.

paperwork.name: Courses of study offered
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190; Ed Code 48222, 51210, 51220 (branches of study)
paperwork.description: A list of the courses/subjects offered each year (e.g., per grade: English, math, social sciences, science, fine arts, health, PE, and for grades 7-12 foreign language etc.), ideally with the curriculum/materials used. Must be kept current and available at the school.

paperwork.name: Faculty names, addresses and educational qualifications
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190; Ed Code 48222 ('persons capable of teaching')
paperwork.description: Names and street addresses of every teacher (usually the parent(s)) with a record of each one's educational qualifications (e.g., diploma/degree, relevant training or experience). No credential is required.

paperwork.name: Immunization records or exemption status
paperwork.legal_basis: H&S Code 120335; 120335(f) exempts pupils in a home-based private school and pupils in independent study (Ed Code 51745 et seq.) who receive no classroom-based instruction
paperwork.description: For a PSA home school serving only the family, and for charter/district independent study with no classroom-based instruction, the school-entry immunization requirements do not apply (CDPH). Keep the child's immunization record anyway: PSPs, charters with in-person classes, co-ops held as classroom instruction, camps, and any later return to a classroom-based school will ask for it. A PSP that is not purely home-based may require records or a valid medical exemption.

paperwork.name: First-grade health examination certificate or waiver (former CHDP form PM 171A/B)
paperwork.deadline: Historically within 90 days after entering first grade (exam within prior 18 months)
paperwork.legal_basis: H&S Code 124085 (text still in code as of Nov 2026); CHDP program ended July 1, 2024 (SB 184, 2022)
paperwork.description: H&S 124085 still requires a certificate of a health screening (or a signed parent waiver) within 90 days of first-grade entry, but it is tied to the CHDP program, which was discontinued July 1, 2024; counties report the PM 171A exam form and PM 171B waiver are no longer required forms. Status for private home schools after the transition is unclear, so keep a copy of the child's well-child exam (or a signed waiver) on file. Public school students (charter/district IS) should follow their school's current instructions; a separate kindergarten/first-grade oral health assessment (Ed Code 49452.8) applies to public schools.

paperwork.name: Criminal record summary / fingerprinting (Ed Code 44237)
paperwork.deadline: Before the employee has contact with pupils
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 44237 (does not apply to a parent or legal guardian working exclusively with his or her own children)
paperwork.description: Private schools must obtain a DOJ criminal record summary for employees who have contact with pupils. A parent teaching only their own children is exempt. If your home school hires a non-parent tutor/teacher or enrolls other families' children, the fingerprinting/background check requirement may apply; keep documentation.

paperwork.name: Withdrawal letter to prior public school
paperwork.deadline: On or before the first day of homeschooling
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 48222 (private school exemption); Ed Code 49068 (records transfer)
paperwork.description: Short written notice to the current school that the child is withdrawing to enroll in a private school (your home-based school, or the named PSP) effective a given date. Prevents truancy follow-up. File the PSA (or enroll in the PSP) before or at the same time. Keep a dated copy and any acknowledgment.

paperwork.name: Cumulative records request to prior school
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 49068 (records transferred on request of the new school)
paperwork.description: Written request from the new school (your private home school, PSP, or charter) asking the former school to transfer the pupil's cumulative record (grades, test scores, immunization and health records, IEP/504 documents). Keep the received records in the student's file.

paperwork.name: PSP enrollment forms and records release
paperwork.frequency: at enrollment and usually re-enrollment each year
paperwork.deadline: Set by the PSP (before the school year or before withdrawing from prior school)
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 / 48222 (PSP files the PSA and keeps records)
paperwork.description: Application/enrollment agreement, parent statement or policies acknowledgment, records request authorization, and any course plan the PSP requires. Confirm the PSP has a current-year PSA on file with CDE.

paperwork.name: Course plan, grades and work logs submitted to PSP
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 33190 (courses of study kept by the school)
paperwork.description: Lists of courses/curricula and end-of-term grades so the PSP can keep the courses-of-study record and issue report cards and high school transcripts.

paperwork.name: Independent study master agreement (charter)
paperwork.frequency: at enrollment; renewed per charter policy (typically each school year)
paperwork.deadline: Signed before independent study instruction begins
paperwork.description: Written agreement signed by the pupil, parent/guardian and supervising teacher covering learning objectives, methods of study and evaluation, how often assignments are due and evaluated, duration, resources, the right to return to classroom instruction, and required synchronous instruction/live interaction. Keep a signed copy.

paperwork.name: Work samples / learning records each learning period (charter)
paperwork.frequency: each learning period (commonly every 20 school days)
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 51747; Ed Code 51747.5 (attendance based on time value of work product); 5 CCR 11703
paperwork.description: Representative samples of student work and/or assignment logs reviewed by the credentialed supervising teacher. These document attendance (ADA) for funding, so missed samples can affect enrollment status. Keep your own copies or photos.

paperwork.name: Independent study agreement and work product (district)
paperwork.frequency: at enrollment and per district schedule
paperwork.deadline: Agreement signed before IS begins; work per district schedule
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 51747; 5 CCR 11700 et seq.
paperwork.description: District written agreement plus completed assignments/work product evaluated by the supervising teacher. Students who fall behind trigger the district's tiered re-engagement procedures required by Ed Code 51747.

paperwork.name: Instructional funds purchase requests and receipts (charter)
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 51747.3 (no funds or thing of value given directly to families); Ed Code 47605 (nonsectarian)
paperwork.description: Requisitions/purchase orders for curriculum, classes and materials bought by the charter through approved vendors with the student's instructional funds. Items are often school property and must be secular. Keep confirmation of each order and any return-of-materials policy.

paperwork.name: Copy of tutor's California teaching credential
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 48224
paperwork.description: Proof that the tutor holds a valid California credential for the grade level taught (printout from the Commission on Teacher Credentialing credential lookup).

paperwork.name: Work permit (Statement of Intent to Employ a Minor and Request for Work Permit, CDE B1-1; Permit to Employ and Work, CDE B1-4)
paperwork.frequency: per job; generally renewed each school year and before the new school year starts
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 49110 et seq.; Labor Code 1286 et seq.
paperwork.description: Minors 12-17 generally need a work permit. Per CDE's FAQ, home schools are private schools, so the principal (or designated administrator who self-certifies knowledge of child labor law) may issue permits, but a principal may NOT issue a permit to his or her own child; in that case (and if the principal declines) the local school district superintendent issues it. PSP students get permits from their PSP; charter and district IS students from their school. Entertainment permits come from the Labor Commissioner (DLSE).

paperwork.name: High school transcript
paperwork.deadline: Final version by graduation; needed for college applications (fall of senior year)
paperwork.legal_basis: No statutory form; private schools set their own graduation requirements (Ed Code 51225.3 applies to public schools)
paperwork.description: Official record of courses, credits, grades and GPA issued by the home-based private school (or by the PSP/charter for those options). Keep course descriptions and reading lists to support it. Retain permanently; former students use the school's records to obtain diplomas/transcripts.

paperwork.name: High school diploma
paperwork.legal_basis: Private school sets its own requirements; alternative: California High School Proficiency Exam certificate (Ed Code 48412)
paperwork.description: The private school (your home school or PSP) issues its own diploma. Students 16+ (or who completed 10th grade) may also take the CHSPE, whose certificate is legally equivalent to a California high school diploma. Charter/district IS students receive their public school's diploma.

paperwork.name: Student cumulative file (grades, test results, portfolio)
paperwork.legal_basis: Best practice (CDE recommends keeping individual pupil records)
paperwork.description: Report cards, standardized test results (if any), samples of work, reading lists, curriculum used and evaluations. Helpful for transfers back to public school, placement, college admissions, and Cal Grant/financial aid documentation.

paperwork.name: State testing and Physical Fitness Test notes
paperwork.legal_basis: Ed Code 60640 (CAASPP) and 60800 (Physical Fitness Test) apply to public schools including charters; not to private schools
paperwork.description: PSA, PSP and tutor students are not required to take CAASPP or the Physical Fitness Test (PFT). Charter and district independent study students participate in CAASPP and, in grades 5, 7 and 9, the PFT. Private homeschoolers may still choose a nationally normed test for their own records.

paperwork.name: Sample letters: withdrawal, records request, notice of exemption
paperwork.description: Templates for a withdrawal letter to the former public school, a cumulative records request from your private school, and a short response to a district or attendance officer inquiry citing Ed Code 48222 and your PSA filing. HSLDA and statewide homeschool organizations publish examples (some member-only).

paperwork.name: Proof of high school completion for financial aid (homeschool)
paperwork.deadline: Cal Grant GPA/test verification by March 2 of senior year; FAFSA/CADAA opens Oct 1
paperwork.legal_basis: 20 U.S.C. 1091(d) (homeschool completion recognized for federal aid when state treats it as a home or private school); CSAC Cal Grant rules
paperwork.description: Keep the final transcript and diploma, plus SAT/ACT or other test scores. Homeschool graduates may substitute accepted test scores for a GPA for Cal Grant purposes, and colleges may request a transcript as proof of homeschool completion for federal aid.

funding.name: Charter school independent study instructional funds
funding.eligibility: Students enrolled in a public charter school's independent study/homeschool program that offers an instructional funds allotment. Not available to PSA, PSP or tutor homeschoolers.
funding.benefit: A per-student budget set by each charter (not by statute) that the school spends on the family's behalf for curriculum, online courses, enrichment classes, lessons, and supplies from approved vendors. Amounts vary by school and grade and can change with the state budget; no official statewide figure exists. Charters receive LCFF funding (2026-27 base grants per ADA: $11,811 TK-3, $10,860 gr 4-6, $11,181 gr 7-8, $13,296 gr 9-12) subject to nonclassroom-based funding determinations.
funding.how_to_apply: Enroll in the charter, sign the independent study master agreement, then submit purchase requests through the charter's ordering system/vendor list with your supervising teacher's approval.
funding.california_notes: Ed Code 51747.3 bars a charter from claiming funding if it gives families funds or anything of value directly, so purchases go through the school and items may remain school property. Public funds cannot buy religious/sectarian materials (charters must be nonsectarian, Ed Code 47605); the challenge Woolard v. Thurmond (9th Cir. decision March 23, 2026) had a cert petition (No. 26-237) distributed for the U.S. Supreme Court's December 4, 2026 conference. Receiving charter funds disqualifies families from some private homeschool grants.

funding.name: HSLDA Curriculum Grant (Compassion)
funding.provider: Home School Legal Defense Association (HSLDA) Compassion / Homeschool Foundation
funding.eligibility: Current HSLDA member; significant financial need; homeschooling at least one child age 6-19 for at least 3 months; funding homeschool privately (not receiving public funds, including ESAs or charter funds); legal custody; most schooling done at home with parent choosing the studies. Can be used for special learning needs resources.
funding.benefit: About $300-$400 per child for curriculum and academic expenses (core curriculum, online class/co-op tuition, testing, tutoring, school-related technology).
funding.how_to_apply: Apply online during an open window: Winter Jan 1-Feb 28, Spring Apr 1-Jun 30, Fall Sep 1-Oct 31 (windows can be shortened or cancelled depending on funds). One application per year; prior recipients submit receipts.
funding.california_notes: California PSA and PSP families qualify; charter and district independent study families do not (public funds).

funding.name: HSLDA Disaster Relief Grant
funding.eligibility: Homeschool families recovering from natural disasters (details on the application page).
funding.benefit: Help with emergency needs and replacement of homeschool goods after a disaster. Amount not published on the overview page.
funding.how_to_apply: Apply through the Disaster Relief Grant application linked from hslda.org/grants.
funding.california_notes: Relevant after California wildfires, floods and earthquakes.

funding.name: HSLDA Membership Financial Aid
funding.eligibility: Homeschool families who cannot afford HSLDA membership.
funding.benefit: Free HSLDA membership, which also makes the family eligible to apply for the Curriculum Grant.
funding.how_to_apply: Apply for Membership Financial Aid via HSLDA (linked from the Curriculum Grant page).
funding.california_notes: Membership gives access to HSLDA's California legal guidance and sample letters.

funding.name: 529 plan K-12 expenses (federal expansion under P.L. 119-21)
funding.provider: Internal Revenue Code section 529 (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, P.L. 119-21, signed July 4, 2025)
funding.eligibility: 529 account beneficiaries with expenses 'in connection with enrollment or attendance at an elementary or secondary public, private, or religious school' (IRC 529(c)(7)).
funding.benefit: Federally tax-free K-12 withdrawals now cover: tuition; curriculum and curricular materials; books or other instructional materials; online educational materials; tutoring or educational classes outside the home by an unrelated qualified tutor (licensed teacher, former eligible-institution teacher, or subject-matter expert); fees for nationally standardized norm-referenced achievement tests, AP exams and college admission exams; dual enrollment fees; and educational therapies for students with disabilities by licensed/accredited practitioners. Expanded expenses apply to distributions after July 4, 2025. Annual K-12 cap rises from $10,000 to $20,000 per beneficiary for taxable years beginning after December 31, 2025 (i.e., 2026 onward).
funding.how_to_apply: Open or use any state's 529 plan; withdraw for qualified K-12 expenses and keep receipts. Report on federal return (Form 1099-Q).
funding.california_notes: The statute does not use the word 'homeschool'; whether a California home-based private school (legally a private school under Ed Code 48222/33190) qualifies is a matter for a tax adviser and IRS guidance. Tutoring must be 'outside the home' and by an unrelated tutor. California does NOT conform: see the ScholarShare entry.

funding.name: California tax treatment of K-12 529 withdrawals / ScholarShare 529
funding.provider: ScholarShare Investment Board / California Franchise Tax Board
funding.eligibility: California taxpayers using any 529 plan (including ScholarShare 529) for K-12 expenses.
funding.benefit: None at the state level for K-12: California has not conformed to the federal K-12 529 rules (since 2018), so the earnings portion of K-12 withdrawals is subject to California income tax plus an additional 2.5% state tax. California also gives no state deduction for 529 contributions. Withdrawals for qualified higher education remain state tax-free.
funding.how_to_apply: Report K-12 withdrawal earnings as income on the California return (FTB Schedule CA / Form 5805 for the 2.5% additional tax); consult a tax professional.
funding.california_notes: The 2025 federal expansion (expanded K-12 categories, $20k limit) does not change California treatment. Pending California bills have not changed K-12 conformity as of Nov 2026 (verify for the current tax year).

funding.name: Coverdell Education Savings Account (ESA)
funding.eligibility: Beneficiary under 18 when contributions are made (or special needs); contributor income limits apply (phase-out traditionally $95,000-$110,000 MAGI single, $190,000-$220,000 joint).
funding.benefit: Up to $2,000 per beneficiary per year in total contributions; earnings tax-free federally when used for qualified elementary and secondary expenses (tuition, books, supplies, equipment, academic tutoring, computer/internet, special needs services) at a 'school' as determined under state law, as well as higher education.
funding.how_to_apply: Open a Coverdell ESA with a bank or brokerage; withdraw for qualified expenses and keep receipts.
funding.california_notes: Because a California home-based private school is a private school under state law, homeschool K-12 expenses may qualify; confirm with a tax adviser. California state tax conformity for Coverdell K-12 withdrawals not confirmed online; check FTB guidance.

funding.name: Federal Tax Credit Scholarship program (Educational Choice for Children, IRC 25F)
funding.provider: U.S. Treasury/IRS via state-approved Scholarship Granting Organizations (SGOs)
funding.eligibility: Donors: individual federal taxpayers. Students: K-12 students in households up to 300% of area median income in states that opt in, through SGOs listed by the state.
funding.benefit: Starting January 1, 2027, a dollar-for-dollar federal tax credit of up to $1,700 per taxpayer per year ($3,400 married filing jointly per advocacy summaries) for donations to SGOs, which fund K-12 scholarships for qualified education expenses.
funding.how_to_apply: Families would apply to an SGO in their state once the state opts in and lists SGOs; donors claim the credit on their federal return.
funding.california_notes: As of late October 2026 Governor Newsom had NOT announced whether California will opt in; the opt-in for tax year 2027 is due by January 1, 2027 (with SGO lists by Feb 15 per reporting). ACR-229 urges opt-in. About 31 states had opted in. If California does not opt in, Californians can still donate to out-of-state SGOs but California students cannot receive these scholarships. Whether homeschool expenses would be covered depends on federal definitions and SGO rules. Re-check status after Jan 1, 2027.

funding.name: Community college special admit (concurrent enrollment) with fee exemption
funding.eligibility: K-12 students recommended by their school principal (for a PSA homeschool, the parent-principal) and with parental consent, admitted as special part-time or full-time students (Ed Code 76001, 48800, 48800.5). Colleges set grade/age, placement and course limits.
funding.benefit: College credit that also counts on the high school transcript. Governing boards may exempt special part-time students (up to 11 units) from the enrollment fee (Ed Code 76300(f)) and they are exempt from nonresident tuition; many districts waive enrollment fees for special part-time students. Special full-time students typically pay fees but may qualify for the California College Promise Grant.
funding.how_to_apply: Submit the CCCApply application plus the college's K-12 special admit/concurrent enrollment form signed by the principal and parent each term.
funding.california_notes: Fee waivers are discretionary and vary by district; homeschool (PSA) students generally use the special admit route rather than CCAP. Under the 2025 federal 529 changes, dual enrollment fees are a qualified K-12 expense federally (not for California tax).

funding.name: College and Career Access Pathways (CCAP) dual enrollment
funding.provider: California Community Colleges in partnership with school districts/charters
funding.eligibility: High school students attending a school district, county office or charter school that has a CCAP partnership agreement with a community college district (Ed Code 76004). Charter and district IS students may qualify through their school; PSA/PSP students generally are not covered.
funding.benefit: Up to 15 units per term; enrollment and student representation fees waived and no fee may be charged that Ed Code 49011 prohibits; priority registration; courses often free of textbook costs per local agreement.
funding.how_to_apply: Ask the charter or district high school counselor which CCAP courses are offered and complete the partnership's enrollment steps.
funding.california_notes: CCAP is created by AB 288 (2015) and was extended/expanded by later bills (e.g., AB 30, 2019). Availability depends entirely on the local partnership.

funding.name: California College Promise Grant (community college enrollment fee waiver)
funding.eligibility: California residents (or AB 540 eligible) meeting income standards, receiving qualifying public assistance, or with financial need per FAFSA/CADAA.
funding.benefit: Waives the per-unit enrollment fee at any California community college.
funding.how_to_apply: Apply via the FAFSA/California Dream Act Application or the College Promise Grant application at the college.
funding.california_notes: Useful for homeschool graduates starting at a community college and, in some districts, for special full-time high school students not covered by special admit fee exemptions.

funding.name: SAT fee waivers (including homeschoolers)
funding.eligibility: Low-income 11th-12th graders (e.g., eligible for free/reduced-price lunch, household income within USDA limits, public assistance). Homeschooled students are eligible.
funding.benefit: Free SAT registrations (typically two), free score sends, and college application fee waivers at participating colleges.
funding.how_to_apply: Homeschoolers may request a waiver directly from College Board via the SAT Fee Waiver Request Form (signed into a College Board account) with proof of eligibility, or through a local high school counselor.
funding.california_notes: Homeschoolers register and test at a public test center.

funding.name: AP Exam fee reduction
funding.eligibility: Students with significant financial need. Homeschooled students may receive the same reductions as other students.
funding.benefit: College Board fee reduction of $37 per AP Exam (schools may also waive their portion); some states add subsidies.
funding.how_to_apply: Homeschoolers arrange to test through the AP coordinator at a school that offers AP exams (contact AP Services for Students for a list); the coordinator applies the reduction.
funding.california_notes: California does not currently offer a separate state AP exam fee subsidy for homeschoolers (not confirmed). Find a host school early in the fall.

funding.name: PSAT/NMSQT for homeschoolers (National Merit Scholarship entry)
funding.provider: College Board / National Merit Scholarship Corporation
funding.eligibility: Homeschooled students (taken in 11th grade for National Merit eligibility) testing at a local school that administers the PSAT/NMSQT.
funding.benefit: Entry into the National Merit Scholarship Program and other scholarship programs; low-income students may receive fee waivers through the host school.
funding.how_to_apply: Contact local high schools months ahead (summer) to arrange to test as a homeschooled student.
funding.california_notes: Arrange with a nearby public or private school; availability of seats varies.

funding.name: Every Kid Outdoors 4th grade pass
funding.provider: U.S. Department of the Interior, USDA Forest Service and partner federal agencies
funding.eligibility: U.S. 4th graders including homeschooled students (and free-choice learners age 10).
funding.benefit: Free entry for the 4th grader and accompanying family (one vehicle at per-vehicle sites) to national parks, forests, wildlife refuges and other federal lands and waters, valid through August 31 of the school year (2026-27 pass valid through August 31, 2027). Does not cover camping or other amenity fees.
funding.how_to_apply: Complete the short online activity at everykidoutdoors.gov and print the voucher (can be exchanged/converted to a digital pass via Recreation.gov).
funding.california_notes: Covers Yosemite, Sequoia/Kings Canyon, Joshua Tree, Death Valley, Redwood, Channel Islands etc. Homeschoolers ARE eligible (unlike the California state parks 4th grade pass).

funding.name: California State Parks Free Fourth Grade Pass (formerly Adventure Pass)
funding.provider: California Department of Parks and Recreation
funding.eligibility: California PUBLIC school 4th graders only (program funded by Proposition 98). Charter and district independent study students are public school students; PSA/PSP homeschool students are NOT eligible.
funding.benefit: Free day-use entry to 54 participating state parks for the student and family, valid up to 13 months (through August 31 of the following year).
funding.how_to_apply: Parent/guardian applies through ReserveCalifornia.com (account required) once sign-up opens in August.
funding.california_notes: Renamed from 'Adventure Pass' (launched 2021 with 19 parks). For PSA/PSP families, use the library parks pass or the federal Every Kid Outdoors pass instead.

funding.name: California State Library Parks Pass
funding.provider: California State Library and California State Parks, via local public libraries
funding.eligibility: Anyone who can check out materials from a participating California public library (no special card needed).
funding.benefit: Free vehicle day-use entry (one vehicle up to 9 people) at 200+ participating state park units; loan period set by each library.
funding.how_to_apply: Place a hold on/check out the Parks Pass from your local public library.
funding.california_notes: Originally a pilot; reporting in 2026 indicates ongoing funding was secured, but confirm with your library. Not valid at units run by other agencies or concessionaires; parking not guaranteed.

funding.name: Discover & Go museum passes
funding.provider: Participating California public library systems (e.g., LA County, San Diego, San Francisco, San Jose, Fresno, Santa Clara County)
funding.eligibility: Adult library cardholders (usually 18+) residing in the library's service area; rules vary by library.
funding.benefit: Free or discounted passes to museums, science centers, zoos and cultural attractions.
funding.how_to_apply: Log in to your library's Discover & Go portal with your card and reserve a pass (typically up to 2 active reservations).
funding.california_notes: Excellent for field trips; combine with homeschool days offered by many museums.

funding.name: Apple education pricing for homeschool teachers
funding.eligibility: Apple's U.S. education terms list homeschool teachers among eligible K-12 educators.
funding.benefit: Education pricing on Macs, iPads and selected accessories (purchase limits apply).
funding.how_to_apply: Buy through the Apple Education Store; Apple may request qualifying information (a copy of your PSA filing is commonly used as proof).
funding.california_notes: Barnes & Noble's former Educator discount (which included homeschool parents) ENDED April 12, 2023; many websites still advertise it. Other retailer teacher discounts vary and change frequently, so verify before relying on them.

funding.name: California LifeLine (phone) and LifeLine Home Broadband Pilot
funding.eligibility: Households enrolled in qualifying programs (e.g., Medi-Cal, CalFresh, LIHEAP) or with income at or below program limits (June 1, 2026-May 31, 2027: $24,600 for 1 person, $33,300 for 2, $42,100 for 3, +$8,700 each additional).
funding.benefit: Discounted home/cell phone service; the Home Broadband Pilot (launched January 26, 2026, three years) gives $20/month off home internet or $30/month off bundled internet+phone with participating providers.
funding.how_to_apply: Apply through California LifeLine (via a participating provider/LifeLine Administrator), then ask a participating ISP to apply the broadband discount. Since Feb 1, 2026, California LifeLine and federal Lifeline require separate enrollments.
funding.california_notes: Replaces some of the help lost when the federal Affordable Connectivity Program ended in 2024.

funding.name: Cal Grant (for homeschool graduates)
funding.eligibility: California residents (or AB 540) with financial need within income/asset ceilings. Cal Grant A generally needs a 3.0 GPA, Cal Grant B a 2.0. Homeschool graduates without a verifiable GPA may substitute accepted test scores (SAT, ACT, GED, HiSET, TASC) or a community college GPA (16+ units).
funding.benefit: Tuition/fee awards at UC, CSU and eligible private colleges; access/living allowance; community college awards.
funding.how_to_apply: File the FAFSA or California Dream Act Application and submit GPA verification (or test scores) by March 2 of senior year (check CSAC for current deadlines and any deadline extensions for community colleges).
funding.california_notes: A PSA home school can submit a GPA verification form as the school; otherwise use the test-score substitution. Keep the transcript and diploma ready.

funding.name: Middle Class Scholarship
funding.eligibility: California undergraduates (and teaching credential students) at UC, CSU or CCC bachelor's degree programs with family income and assets each up to the annual ceiling (e.g., $234,000 for 2025-26 per UC San Diego); FAFSA/CADAA required. No high school GPA requirement known.
funding.benefit: Sliding-scale scholarship toward remaining cost of attendance based on income and other aid received.
funding.how_to_apply: File the FAFSA or California Dream Act Application by the CSAC deadline; no separate application.
funding.california_notes: Homeschool graduates are evaluated like other undergraduates once enrolled at UC/CSU.

funding.name: Federal Student Aid (Pell Grant, etc.) for homeschool graduates
funding.eligibility: Students who completed secondary school in a homeschool setting treated as a home or private school under state law are eligible for federal aid (20 U.S.C. 1091(d)).
funding.benefit: Pell Grants, work-study and federal loans.
funding.how_to_apply: File the FAFSA (opens October 1); indicate homeschool completion. Colleges may ask for a transcript or other completion evidence.
funding.california_notes: A California PSA home school is a private school under Ed Code 48222, so graduates qualify.

funding.name: Jack Kent Cooke Foundation College Scholarship
funding.eligibility: High school seniors with unmet financial need (family income up to $95,000 considered), minimum unweighted GPA 3.75, SAT/ACT/AP/IB scores; homeschooled students are explicitly eligible.
funding.benefit: One of the largest undergraduate scholarships in the U.S., covering a substantial share of college costs for up to four years, plus advising (check jkcf.org for the current maximum award).
funding.how_to_apply: Online application, typically opening in August with a fall deadline.
funding.california_notes: No state restriction.

funding.name: Davidson Fellows Scholarship
funding.eligibility: Students 18 or younger as of the deadline (no minimum age; based on age, not grade) who complete a significant project in STEM, literature, music or philosophy; U.S. citizen or permanent resident. No school-type restriction found, so homeschoolers apply under the same rules.
funding.benefit: Scholarships of $10,000, $25,000 or $50,000.
funding.how_to_apply: Online application; the 2027 cycle opens fall 2026 with a February 2027 deadline (exact date to be posted by Davidson).
funding.california_notes: Well suited to project-based homeschool learners.

funding.name: No state-funded California homeschool grant or ESA
funding.eligibility: N/A
funding.benefit: California has no education savings account, voucher, or state grant program for private homeschoolers (PSA/PSP). Public funding reaches homeschooling families only through enrollment in charter or district independent study.
funding.how_to_apply: N/A
funding.california_notes: Watch for a California decision on the federal tax-credit scholarship program (opt-in deadline January 1, 2027).
